title: Soft-wash chemicals, SDS and exposure boundaries
audience: Trainee or new worker on the roof soft washing track, working under supervision.
learningOutcomes: Identify conditions, authorisation limits and evidence requirements relevant to soft-wash chemicals, sds and exposure boundaries.
Differentiate worker-observable conditions from determinations reserved to qualified roof, electrical, chemical or environmental specialists.
Demonstrate a proportionate stop-work, referral and documented client communication using a paper-based scenario.

instruction.heading: Why the chemical question is an authority question
instruction.body: Chemicals are the reason soft washing is different from a simple rinse. Each product carries its own hazards to the operator, to people nearby, to plants and water features, and to the environment. A product that is approved for one method may be wrong for another, and a mixture that has never been tested may react in a way nobody planned for. The question of which product may be used, in what concentration, by whom and where, is therefore an authority question as well as a technical one. A worker does not settle it by reading a label on the truck or by accepting a supplier's description. This lesson shows how to check the paperwork, set the boundary around the work, and stop when the evidence is missing.

instruction.heading: Reading a safety data sheet
instruction.body: A safety data sheet, or SDS, is the document that describes a chemical's hazards and how to handle it safely. Manufacturers and importers are responsible for preparing it, and it must describe the hazards, safe handling, storage and disposal, physical and chemical properties, health effects, emergency response and environmental effects. It follows a standard set of headings. When you use an SDS, start with the product identification, the hazard identification and the first-aid measures. Then read the handling and storage sections, the exposure controls and personal protection, the stability and reactivity information, which names the materials to keep apart, and the spill, disposal and environmental sections. Check that the product name and concentration on the SDS match the container label. Check the review date shown on the SDS, because the Safe Work Australia guidance says that SDSs must be reviewed and updated at least every five years. An SDS that is out of date or does not match the product is not an SDS for that product.

instruction.heading: The hazardous chemicals register
instruction.body: A business or site that uses hazardous chemicals should keep a hazardous chemicals register. Safe Work Australia's guidance says the register lists only hazardous chemicals, includes the current SDS for each listed chemical, is kept up to date, and is kept at the workplace where it can be reached easily. Workers, anyone who could be affected, and emergency services should be able to use it. Non-hazardous chemicals are not listed, and some hazardous consumer products and chemicals in transit are excluded, but the guidance says that chemicals in transit may still need listing if they are present in large amounts or stored often. Safety information for every chemical at the workplace, hazardous or not, must still be available. In practice, the label and the SDS carry that information. The register does not replace the duty to share it.

instruction.heading: Products, mixing and incompatibility
instruction.body: Use only the products on the authorised product list for the job, and use them only in the way the label and the approved method describe. No dilution rate is given in this lesson. Any dilution comes from the label and the approved method, and the worker does not work it out from memory. Do not mix two products, even two that are sold for cleaning, unless the label, the SDS and the authorised method all allow it. Mixing can produce a reaction that is hazardous in itself, such as a gas release, and the SDS names the materials to keep apart. Keep containers closed when they are not in use, keep them labelled, and never decant one product into an unlabelled bottle. If two products arrive on the same truck and the crew wants to combine them in one tank to save time, the answer is no. Separate them, hold the work, and refer the question to the decision owner.

instruction.heading: Setting the exposure boundary
instruction.body: An exposure boundary is the area within which people, animals, plants, vehicles, water features and drains could be affected by the product or the run-off. It is set on the plan before any product is handled, not by eye on the day. Mark the wash area, then extend the boundary to cover the places the product or spray could reach, taking account of wind direction, the layout of the building and the paths people use. Check for a swimming pool, a rainwater tank, a garden bed, a pond, parked vehicles, a play area, and any stormwater pit or drain on the property or the footpath. Put up barriers and signs where needed, and keep the public out until the authorised method and the product's label say the area can be reopened. Whether the boundary is set, and whether the work can go ahead, is the decision of the authorised approver. A worker records the boundary and does not decide it alone.

instruction.heading: PPE, first aid and spill response
instruction.body: Personal protective equipment is chosen from the SDS and the risk assessment, not from habit. Many products call for eye protection and gloves, and some call for protective clothing. Respiratory protection is used only where the SDS and the risk assessment call for it. Keep the first-aid instructions from the SDS on site and make them known to the crew. Keep a spill kit that matches the products on the job, and know how to use it. Other first-aid advice found in older roofing handbooks, such as household neutralising agents, is not adopted in this lesson, because the first-aid measure for each product is the one on its SDS. If someone is exposed, follow the SDS, call emergency services where the SDS or the situation requires it, and report the incident under the business's procedure.

instruction.heading: Storage, transport and waste
instruction.body: Store chemicals in their original, labelled containers, keep incompatible products apart, and keep them out of reach of the public and away from heat and sunlight. Transport them upright and secured, and check that the vehicle carries the spill kit. Do not pour unused product or rinse water into a drain, a stormwater pit, a garden or a water feature. Dispose of unused product and empty containers as the SDS and the local rules describe. Hold the work and refer any disposal question to the decision owner.

instruction.heading: When paperwork is missing
instruction.body: A product without a current SDS, without a clear label, or without an approved method is not ready to use, however familiar it looks. A supplier's assurance, a photograph of the front of the container or a verbal description is not an SDS. If the SDS is missing, hold the product, request the current SDS from the supplier or the manufacturer, check the hazardous chemicals register, and tell the decision owner. Record the date of the request and the reply. Do not test the product on a small area to see how it behaves, because that is an application, and it is not authorised by this lesson.

procedure: Identify each product on the job pack by name, concentration and container label, and record any product that is not on the authorised list.
Obtain the current SDS for each product, check that its name and concentration match the label, and record the version and review date.
Read the SDS sections on hazards, first aid, handling, personal protection, stability and incompatible materials, spill response and disposal, and record any gap.
Check the hazardous chemicals register and confirm that the current SDS is held at the workplace.
Hold any product without a current SDS or an approved method, and tell the decision owner.
Mark the exposure boundary on the site plan, including people, pets, plants, vehicles, water features, tanks and drains, and record the run-off path.
Confirm the PPE, ventilation and spill kit required by the SDS and the label before anyone handles the product.
Record the decision, the SDS version and date, the boundary, and the people informed, before any product is opened.

workedExamples.situation: A supplier sends a photo of a new cleaner's front label and says it is the same as the product the crew already uses. No safety data sheet is attached.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the crew use the product, and what is recorded?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. A front label and a verbal assurance are not an SDS, and the product is not approved on the job pack. Hold the product, request the current SDS from the supplier or manufacturer, and check the hazardous chemicals register. Record the photograph, the supplier's statement, the request and the reply, and tell the decision owner. Do not test the product to see whether it is the same, because that is an application.

workedExamples.situation: A crew has two products on the truck. To save time they want to combine them in one tank for a single pass over a roof and its gutters.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the correct decision, and what is the next step?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not combine them. Mixing is allowed only where the label, the SDS and the authorised method all allow it, and nothing here confirms that. Separate the products, check the SDS sections on stability and incompatible materials, and hold the work until the decision owner has reviewed the question. Record the request, the decision and the reason.

workedExamples.situation: A soft wash is planned for a home with a swimming pool, a rainwater tank close to the eave, a garden bed on the boundary, and children playing in the back yard on Saturday.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Where is the exposure boundary set, and who decides whether the work goes ahead?
workedExamples.reasoning: The boundary is set on the plan before any product is handled. It must take in the pool, the tank, the garden bed and the play area, and it must consider wind direction and the run-off path to the drains. Children and pets must be kept out, and the boundary must be marked. Whether the work may go ahead on Saturday with those features present is the decision of the authorised approver, not the crew's. Record the boundary, the people and features affected, the question sent to the approver, and the answer.

equipmentAndPpe: The current SDS for each product, held on site or available on request, with its version and review date recorded.
The authorised product list for the job, and the product labels.
PPE chosen from the SDS: eye protection, gloves and protective clothing, and respiratory protection only where the SDS and the risk assessment require it.
A spill kit that matches the products on the job, and a first-aid kit with the SDS first-aid instructions.
Barriers, signs and marking material for the exposure boundary.
A site plan showing the boundary, drains, tanks, pools, plants, vehicles and the run-off path.

commonErrors.error: Treating a product label as a safety data sheet.
commonErrors.prevention: Request the current SDS and check its name, concentration, version and review date against the label.
Do not mix products unless the label, the SDS and the authorised method all allow it. Hold the question for the decision owner.

commonErrors.error: Setting the exposure boundary by eye on the day.
commonErrors.prevention: Set the boundary on the plan before work, and include pools, tanks, drains, plants, vehicles and children.

commonErrors.error: Relying on an SDS whose review date or product details do not match.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the version, review date and product name before relying on the SDS. Request a current copy if they do not match.

commonErrors.error: Letting run-off reach a stormwater drain, a pond or a garden.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the run-off path before work. Hold the work if the path cannot be controlled.

commonErrors.error: Assuming a product is safe because it is sold for household use.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only the authorised products, and apply the PPE, first aid and disposal steps from the SDS, not from the consumer packaging.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Licence and authority notice: This lesson does not grant a licence, certificate, accreditation or authority to apply chemicals, to dilute products, or to carry out any regulated work. Check your state or territory rules before any application.

SDS duties: Safe Work Australia's guidance on safety data sheets says manufacturers and importers must prepare them, that an SDS must cover hazards, safe handling, storage and disposal, physical and chemical properties, health and emergency response, and environmental effects, and that each SDS must be reviewed and updated at least every five years, with the last review date shown. The page does not set out the employer's duty to keep SDSs available to workers, and refers the reader to the state or territory WHS regulator.

Hazardous chemicals register: Safe Work Australia's guidance says a register must list the hazardous chemicals used or stored at a workplace, include the current SDS for each, be kept up to date and be accessible at the workplace. Large stored quantities may need a separate manifest. The state or territory regulator's rules should be checked.

Incompatible products: Products must not be mixed unless the label, the SDS and the authorised method allow it. The SDS names incompatible materials, and that information must be followed. No dilution or mixing instruction in this lesson is a substitute for the label or the approved method.
Environmental discharge: Run-off and waste must not enter a stormwater drain, a garden or a water feature. Hold the work where run-off cannot be controlled.

Public exposure: Children, pets, neighbours and passers-by must be kept outside the exposure boundary during application and until the authorised method and the label allow the area to reopen. The approver, not the crew, decides whether the work can go ahead when people or features are close to the boundary.

Stop-work rule: Stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if a product has no current SDS or approved method, if two products are to be mixed without approval, if the boundary has not been set or people are inside it, if run-off cannot be controlled, or if the task falls outside your authorisation.

qualityStandard: Each product on the job has a current SDS whose name, concentration, version and review date match the container label, and the details are recorded.
Any product without a current SDS or an approved method is held, and no application takes place.
No products are mixed unless the label, the SDS and the authorised method all allow it, and the decision is recorded.
The exposure boundary is marked on the site plan before work, and it includes people, pets, plants, vehicles, water features, tanks and drains.
PPE, first-aid instructions and the spill kit required by the SDS are in place before any product is handled.
The run-off path is recorded, and any path that cannot be controlled holds the work.
documentationEvidence: A product register with each product's name, concentration, SDS version, review date and approval status.
A copy of each SDS used, held on site or available to the crew, with the date it was obtained.
A site plan showing the exposure boundary, the features within it, and the run-off path.
A PPE and spill-kit check recorded before handling, and the SDS first-aid instructions noted.
A hold or approval record for any product, showing the request, the reply and the decision owner.
summary: A product label is not a safety data sheet. Check the current SDS against the label, including its name, concentration and review date.
Products are not mixed, and no dilution is worked out from memory. The label, the SDS and the authorised method decide.
The exposure boundary is set on the plan before work and must include people, pets, plants, water features and drains.
A missing SDS, an unapproved product or an uncontrolled run-off path holds the work. The decision belongs to the approver.

knowledgeChecks.question: A supplier sends a photo of a product's front label but no safety data sheet. What should happen?
options: Use the product, because the label names the active ingredient clearly on the front of the bottle
Hold the product, request the current SDS, and do not apply it until the SDS has been reviewed.
Ask the client to approve the product and proceed with the whole wash on the roof today
Test a small patch and treat the result as the safety data sheet itself for the whole job

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement about mixing products is correct?
options: Two products may be mixed if both are sold for cleaning on the same roof, job or site
Mixing is fine if the tank is rinsed afterwards with clean water from the hose today
Products are not mixed unless the label, the SDS and the authorised method all allow it.
The operator decides on the day whether mixing is safe for the roof and the wash plan

knowledgeChecks.question: Which date on a safety data sheet should a worker check before relying on it?
options: The date the product was first manufactured and placed on the shelf
The date the SDS was last reviewed, and whether it is the current version.
The date of the last job at this site and who did it on the day
The date printed on the bottle cap and the lid of the container

knowledgeChecks.question: Where should the exposure boundary be set for a soft wash near a pool, a rainwater tank and a garden?
options: At the wash area only, where the spray is aimed and where the crew stands during the whole wash on the roof today, and nowhere else
At the nearest fence line only, since that is the edge of the property and the neighbour's yard, and the wash does not reach beyond it
Using the authorised method and the SDS, covering people, pets, plants, vehicles, water features and drains that could be affected.
Wherever the worker feels comfortable on the day, since they know the site and the roof best of all people involved
